utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd first like to put on the record that two declarations of waiver of the right to be present for both accused were received and were filed. Therefore, we'll proceed in the absence of both accused. The next item which does not appear on the agenda you may have received is the matter of the draft medical protocol. It primarily concerns the Stanisic Defence. I don't know whether you want to proceed in open session, Mr. Jordash, or whether you would prefer to proceed in closed session. The first question is that since you've received it only very recently, whether you want to make any submissions on what is still very much a draft of a protocol which is considered in the context of exploring possibilities. So there is no definitive status of it, but I do not know whether you want to make any observations at this moment or whether you'd like to delay that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I delay that until tomorrow or Friday. I think tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not sitting -- if we finish today, we'll not sit on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. And if I can make the submissions by e-mail or by formal response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you make a -- I don't know what the content will be, but you can make it a confidential filing. The reason why I pushed it -- we hoped, as a matter of fact, to present it to you already at an earlier stage, but there were some problems involved which -- which didn't allow us to bring it to your attention any earlier. Important is that now you've seen the draft that perhaps you already include that in any discussions you may have with the Republic of Serbia. This is not a final document, but at least for first orientation it might assist, because you may have noticed that it's also slightly different from the usual conditions. Further, if you look at it, and without inviting you now to -- to make further submissions, but if this finally would be adopted or a similar thing would be adopted, then it might be -- in order to make it work, it might be good if there would be a written waiver of patient/doctor privilege, because in the system there's a monitoring system in which we expect all doctors to give all information they have if need be. Then, of course, especially if you're not in a position which is still a possibility to give that waiver at that moment, then it's -- I think it would be good to have already a written waiver in advance. And I'd like you to consider that already, apart from any other observations you may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. Having quickly read it, I doubt we will have any observations, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We will then -- we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. As the parties may be aware, there are some difficulties with the functioning of Courtroom II, which requires some flexibility and some adaptation by the Trial Chambers. Initially it looked as if we could not sit next week Tuesday; that's the 5th. But the situation has now changed, and we can sit on Tuesday the 5th, however, not in the afternoon but only in the morning. Therefore, the 5th of October session will be in the morning, not in the afternoon. Any comments on -- then I move on to the next point, which is the bar table motion. The Stanisic Defence has indicated by -- in an e-mail of the 23rd of September, an e-mail addressed to the parties and to the Chamber, that it will file a detailed written response to the bar table motion by Friday, the 1st of October. Is that still to be expected, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think what we intended to say, and I think this was -- we apologise for this, we intended to say that we would file a response with the Prosecution by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I'd understood. And then your response would be worked into the spreadsheet so that I think that we would expect the spreadsheet to be filed not later than the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask for a slightly longer period, but only by a few days. If we could have until Wednesday next to file that response. There are a lot of documents, and there's been a lot to go through on other issues, and we are running a bit late, but we are on the way, and we can certainly have it done by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wednesday would be the 6th of October? Because the Chamber had on its mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we noticed that the Prosecution has developed great skills in working in your comments in their spreadsheets. If it's delivered in such a way that it's a matter of copying, then we could still perhaps then have the spreadsheet being filed on the 6th of October, which was, as a matter of fact, the deadline the Chamber had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Adam Weber on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That can be done. It would be helpful if the spreadsheet could arrive with the Prosecution in the earlier portion of the day, and it would also be helpful if we could get the Simatovic Defence comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Noon, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you indicated that you would finish that job Friday. You'll have until Wednesday noon. And then the Prosecutor will import all your comments into the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I haven't heard -- we haven't heard any commitment from the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, we wish to do the same, to forward our complete submission by Wednesday, noon, if that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, working in two responses doesn't take much more time than on response, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but may I take it that you'll organise it in such a way that you deliver your comments in the most -- I would say in the -- in such a format that it will take as little time as possible for Mr. Weber to work it into the spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution receives it in a similar table that we provided in a Word format, we can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll proceed. And the Chamber sets a deadline for the Defences to provide their information to the Prosecution at Wednesday, the 6th of October, at noon. And we expect the table to be filed on that same day. The next item on my agenda is the report of Robert Donia. The Defence wished to -- to make submissions on it. Do you prefer to do that orally or in writing, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It would probably be most efficient to do it in writing in the first instance. I had intended to indicate to the Prosecution precisely which paragraphs we object to. They relate to one chapter of the report, the "Conduct of War" chapter. And it may be, once we've indicated that - and I could indicate that in the next half an hour - that we may be able to come to an agreement and save court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there's no disagreement, you would prefer to make your submissions in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The submissions -- either way, Your Honour. They're very short submissions about relevance of excerpts relating to Sarajevo and Srebrenica mainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I also hear from the Simatovic Defence what their position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I recollect correctly, I don't think we had any objections in this part, hence I believe this item on the agenda only has to do with the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear then. I suggest the following: That during the first break, Mr. Jordash, that you briefly confer with the Prosecution, that you see whether the problems can be resolved. If not, it will depend on the time available after the break whether we'll invite you to make those oral submissions or whether we would invite you to make written submissions. You say they'll be very short. Could you give us a more precise indication of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Ten minutes, I think, from the Defence perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. And would that also mean that if we do not find time today, and I would not convene another session tomorrow just merely for this, that -- well, let's see, you're busy with the bar table until Wednesday, that we could receive your brief submissions not any later than next week Friday? Is that ... Okay. So you try to seek a solution. We'll see whether we have time today. If not, you'll have filed your submissions by Friday, the 7th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 8th, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 8th. Yes. Yes. Tuesday's the 5th. The 8th, yes. By Friday, the 8th of October. We now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Donia report. Any agreement in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No agreement as such. We've indicated the paragraphs. And if there's time, I could make very quick general submissions on -- on the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do not mind, we'll leave that to the end. I see how quickly or slowly we're moving on. We have already a date set if there's no time for the submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we've spoken to Mr. Groome. We're quite happy to do it by -- in writing as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, the Chamber prefers then to receive them in writing, not later than the 8th of October. That was the -- yes. I know that that's a Friday. Yes. Which reminds me that I don't think, as a matter of fact, that the Donia report has received -- has been assigned a number. Could the parties assist me in giving the 65 ter number. It has been filed as an expert report, and to that extent it's part of the record, but it has not received an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 5396. Madam Registrar, that should be a report by Mr. Robert Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1483 is marked for identification pending a decision on admission. We move on. The -- there is a missing document associated to Mr. Deronjic's evidence, which is a pending issue. Now, I do not know whether we have to move into private session for that or not, Mr. Groome, but the Chamber would like to hear, as requested on the 22nd of September by you, to hear oral submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe we need to be in private session for this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what you're going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're invited to make your oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are we in open is session now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1684 was part of the original Prosecution 65 ter list filed on the 2nd of April, 2007. Despite the fact that this is a 92 quater related exhibit associated with the evidence of Miroslav Deronjic, it was inadvertently omitted from the Prosecution 65 ter list filed on 1st of May, 2009. The corrigendum to the 92 quater motion for Mr. Deronjic, which was filed on the 7th of October, 2009, lists 65 ter 1684 among the related exhibits. This is purely a clerical error, and the Prosecution moves to reinstate the document to its 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are exclusively talking about adding it to the -- or re-introducing it to the 65 ter list. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that a key issue was not resolved in relation to 92 quater, anything in relation to the witness that is requested under that Rule is something that we strongly object to. Anything that has to do with the testimony that is sought to be tendered cannot be dealt with in such a way. I believe our objection should stand and that there be no admittance of the testimony of those 92 quater witnesses. Anything that would be introduced through that procedure is something that this Defence would object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I do not fully see is how that justifies not to add it to the 65 ter list. I mean, it would be an associated exhibit, and it would, as an associated exhibit to be dealt with in close connection with -- of course, the main issue. But we would have to do it -- to go through the same route twice but then for a separate document. So therefore it's not entirely clear to me, but -- I see that you object against admission of the Deronjic evidence under Rule 92 quater. That's clear. And this decision, I would say, is -- I can't say fully unrelated to, but of course nothing is lost if it's added to the 65 ter list where it will find a place close to -- to the Deronjic testimony, and that's -- of course, will be considered in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our position is that of principle. Of course you are correct, but that way of introducing anything that has to do with it -- well, I understand that this does not prejudice your decision, but any kind of that type of procedure is something we strongly object to on principle grounds. It is up to you to decide whether that document will be reinstated onto the 65 ter list. I just wanted to make our position clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We -- we understand the concerns of the Simatovic team. On the other hand, we also acknowledge what Your Honour has said about there being no prejudice, and therefore we take no position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only prejudice possible is whether you have got sufficient notice. Now, if we do not admit the evidence, that is, of course, a totally different matter. The 65 ter list is there in order to avoid surprises, and that's, of course -- that's the issue which is now at stake, rather than anything else, and not a fundamental discussion on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add 65 ter 1684 to the 65 ter list without -- this in -- not in any way anticipates the decision of this Chamber on the admission into evidence of the evidence given by Mr. Deronjic under Rule 92 quater. The next item is -- yes. That's -- that's the item I confused earlier with -- the payment records. The Chamber asked the Prosecution to file a completed spreadsheet table by today, I think at noon. That has been -- no, even -- yes. On -- to be filed on Tuesday. That was done. I've seen that. The Stanisic observations are included now in that table. There appears to be no response from the Simatovic Defence, so therefore at this moment nothing is found in this chart as relation to possible objections from the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. In the accompanying submission, our learned friend stated our position which we provided at page 5154 of the transcript. Our position vis-à-vis these documents have to do with probative value. We will, accordingly, argument our position in the procedure in the latter course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that you do not object admission at this moment, but that you'll -- at a later stage you will argue that they are without probative value?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which would be -- if they really are without, it would be an admissibility problem as well, because we're supposed to admit evidence which has at least some probative value. But you'd rather say it has no weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is difficult to say at this moment. It is beyond dispute that they were received from the state based on an RFA, and it is not in dispute that they are authentic. It is therefore difficult to analyse it any further from this position. I'm afraid I cannot argument our position objecting to their admission right away. However, once we have studied it all, we will appropriately deal with all the aspects of that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is all rather vague in terms of time. Clearly, do you at this moment oppose admission, apart from whether that you'll argue at a later stage that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we find the position of the Stanisic Defence on the chart by now? Yes. Then I have a few more questions. I think that the chart now exists of 56 exhibits in total, of which 25 have already exhibit numbers, but there are still quite a number without. So before we'll deal with the matter first, we have to get our administrative activities well organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sent an e-mail to your legal officers yesterday indicating that we'd like to develop our submissions if we may, especially in light of the Prosecution's submissions in the joint filing. We hadn't expected the Prosecution to put partisan submissions in the filing above and beyond that which was in the table, and we would like to address the issue of notice in relation to these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I can imagine that you're specifically concerned about being blamed for now taking a position which you supposedly had given up already at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's part of it. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I could complete the submissions in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. We'll do hear this -- Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would just ask leave, then, to have the opportunity to respond to the submissions made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I put the ten-minute submissions on my list. If we find time today, without violating the fundamental rights of interpreters, transcribers, et cetera, you will have an opportunity to do that. And then Mr. Weber can respond to that. If we do not find it today, apparently I've prepared it that you're -- then you're invited, since we're not sitting -- or most likely when we're sitting the 4th and the 5th we might not find time to do these kind of things. And instead of calling another session tomorrow, it's either ten minutes today or the 8th of October, that same Friday. But if you want until the 10th or 11th, then -- but apparently you have prepared for it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I would still, I think, prefer to have the 10th or the 11th if we don't get to it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 11th, Mr. Jordash, which is a Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just in terms of facilitating scheduling, the Prosecution right now, based on the comments in chart and the expected arguments by the Stanisic Defence, would also approximate 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So I have -- if we don't have 20 minutes left today, then we will leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was only -- I was leaping to my feet because I'm responding to the Prosecution's submissions. And I don't want to be overly technical about and insist upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see. Most likely -- most likely we find no time for it anyhow because we have this still long MFI list. And then you can write, as long as you stay within the limits of the practice direction for filings. Let's be -- let's move on. The next item is the testimony of Mr. Theunens, which I have on my list. He's now scheduled, as matters stand now, the end of October. The Prosecution has announced that it will timely provide B/C/S audio files of the Theunens -- of the testimony he's expected to give in the Sljivancanin case in order to be in compliance with Rule 66(A)(ii) which imposes an obligation to provide the other party with statements of witnesses. It will take some time, you say. Could you give an indication, Mr. Groome, as what "some time" means?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. It's a matter that's outside of our control. We will speak with the director assigned that day and see if it's possible to at the same moment create a copy that we can then provide. The issue that I wanted to raise is it seems clear to me that both accused speak English. I've spoken to the appeals counsel on this matter. The Appeals Chamber has allocated one hour for Prosecution and for Defence for questioning Mr. Theunens, and his evidence relates to Vukovar and Ovcara, matters not concerned with this case. So my question was whether the -- the Defence teams would accept the English transcription, whether their clients would agree to read the English in lieu of the tape, and we will, of course, pursue -- attempt to get the tape as soon as we can. The other possibility that occurred to me is that arrangements could be made so that the two accused can actually watch the proceedings via the videolink that's already established, and that way they could also hear it in their own language prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems a very practical solution, especially when it's expected that the relevance of what Mr. Theunens will testify about may be very limited for our case. And I do not know whether the other parties share that view, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure we share the view that what Mr. Theunens will say in that case will be of limited relevance. I recall the Prosecution's position in relation to Vukovar being that the indictment alleges forcible transfer in Vukovar. In fact, the Prosecution have insisted, constantly insisted, upon leading evidence relating to that. Your Honours will recall the evidence led --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. You disagree with the Prosecution in that respect. Now, if we're talking about solutions, what -- would it be sufficient for two hours of evidence -- would you prefer to have the your clients - and I'm also addressing Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Petrovic - to have an opportunity for your clients to follow the proceedings? And that would be possible in -- in B/C/S also or just in English? I take it B/C/S would also be one of the channels that could be received in the UNDU.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Direct --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that on the 12th of -- 12th of October, where we do not expect Mr. Theunens to testify any earlier than the very end of October, what would you further need if a B/C/S transcript would not be immediate -- B/C/S audio would not be available immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just inquire as to whether the position is that the B/C/S tape would not be available before Mr. Theunens came in this case, which is a full 13 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that it will be there in a couple of days but not on the 12th itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm quite confident it will be available before. I just -- I don't know how much time the two accused would like to review it and then instruct their counsel, and that's why I made this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't -- I think the proposal seems to be a good one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will receive immediately the English version. The accused will have an opportunity - this is to be organised, of course, with the United Nations Detection Unit - to follow the proceedings in Sljivancanin in their own language. And then as soon as the B/C/S audio would be available, it could be provided, but then the time pressure is less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is acceptable for us as well, but I think that the tape would probably be available a couple of days later, at least that is what happened in the previous -- in previous cases. So in this matter, I think that we don't expect to have any major problems or objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the Chamber likes to hear. We move on to the -- everything is said about this, Mr. Groome, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just query whether the Chamber wishes the Prosecution to explore that with the Detention Unit or will the Chamber instruct the Registrar to make some inquiries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the Registry to first explore the possibility to inform you, and I think it can be dealt with. And if they need your assistance, they'll let you know. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I also raise at this stage, in relation to Mr. Theunens, that having got further into preparation for that witness, I think our original estimate may have been somewhat conservative. I think I said to Your Honour during the informal meeting that we would require between five to ten hours of cross-examination time. I cannot, having looked at the report further, imagine cross-examining Mr. Theunens for less than around eight hours and more likely in excess of ten hours, up to 15. I indicate that now. I've made inquiries with the Prosecution about Mr. Theunens' availability the week after, and we await for the results of that inquiry. I thought I'd better raise that so that there's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please keep the Chamber informed about it. I think the first one who becomes unhappy is the boss of Mr. Theunens rather than anyone in this courtroom, at this moment at least. I'm not saying that that will remain the same. And as always, Mr. Jordash -- first of all, it's good that you already announce that this might be a witness which requires more time than usual and to give an indication of that. Second, the Chamber always carefully monitor how time in cross-examination is used in order to finally determine how to proceed and how many time finally will be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it would probably be useful to know what the estimate is from our team. I looked at a large number of documents from the Croatian collection, which has to do with documents that are being admitted through this expert, and I think that the presenting of those documents will take a lot of time. So our Defence will probably need between eight to ten hours also. Of course, if it's still too early to be able to make some kind of agreement and to work out things at this point in time, but if Mr. Jordash were to cover the majority of the topics, then that would shorten our time. But I would kindly ask that you reserve as much time for our team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has two elements. First of all, whether the Chamber grants such time for cross-examination. That's -- we can't say anything about that at this very moment. The second is that Mr. Groome should take this into account for further scheduling and preparing for calling witnesses. That's -- these are the two items. And you're more or less the last one in line, Mr. Groome. We move on. The first joint motion for admission of agreed facts between the Prosecution and the Stanisic Defence which was filed on the 16th of February. The Prosecution requests the admission into evidence of Annex A to that motion. The matter has been further discussed. The Stanisic Defence has filed the Stanisic Defence assent on the 22nd of February. The issue was further discussed in court on the 25th of May. And on the 2nd of June of 2010, the Chamber has declared the crime-based part -- the Croatian crime-based part moot. That was because most of the evidence was already admitted through Witnesses Pilic and Strinovic. Now, the Trial Chamber then invited for a joint filing, and the Chamber would like to receive that filing -- well, let's see, Stanisic Defence apparently is ready. Simatovic Defence has never presented its position on the matter, although it's pending for quite a long time. When do you think you could provide your positions to the Prosecution so as to prepare for a joint filing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're doing our utmost. But in the coming couple of weeks, there's a whole lot of things that we need to do, including meet our administrative obligations vis-à-vis the secretariat relating to the end-of-stage report, but we will kindly ask that this deadline be some seven days after the testimony of expert witness Theunens. We are able to undertake that commitment, that we will be able to meet this obligation of ours in that deadline seven days after the testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, first of all, we do not know exactly when the testimony will be. Second, you both announced that you would take considerable more time, well, let's say 20 hours in addition to the Prosecution's time. We are close to Christmas if -- we have to cancel the ordering of our turkeys for Christmas if it -- I had on my mind, Mr. Petrovic, to grant three weeks. I'm willing to extend that so that you have five weeks from now, which means that you have time to prepare for Mr. Theunens, most likely, if he testifies at the end of October, but at the same time we're for the going to wait necessarily until he has finished his testimony, also in view of all the uncertainties. Five weeks, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five weeks is sufficient, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I didn't ask you because agreed facts you rather know them at the beginning of the trial rather than at the end. Any comments in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- I just wanted to return to the scheduling of Mr. Theunens. On that week that he's scheduled to testify, the Court is scheduled to sit two days. The Prosecution would request, given the new estimate, if it were possible for the Chamber to explore having hearings for an additional two days. We are off -- there's a UN holiday on the 25th, the Monday of that week, but if we were able to sit for the remaining days of that week. I do know Mr. Theunens does have the scheduling problems that were discussed at length at our informal meeting. I know it will be his preference to do this all in one week. We will, of course, explore other options, but it would be very helpful if we were able to sit additional hearings that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just for my information, you scheduled Mr. Theunens for how many hours again? Four hours, which I considered certainly not too pessimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was our original estimate, and Your Honour will recall we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You reduced that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We think that we will be substantially reducing that. It depends on some of the negotiations with Defence with respect to some of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have -- well, two times eight to ten hours. Depending on how that would be, another 16 to 20 hours, 24 hours. 24 hours of evidence doesn't fit in four days. Even -- even if we would agree to four days a week, whereas we actually did agree to three days a week, we do not know -- there are quite a bit of uncertainties, but I do not see how we could -- if we would grant the request of the Defence, how we could fit 20 hours or more in one week, because in our calculations, it's three and a half effective hours a day, and if we are very efficient, we can make that close to four.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't suggest that it would -- that there would be enough time to do his entire testimony. What I'm simply saying, it was -- it would reduce the logistical problems he faces if in that week that he appears we were able to make maximum use of the time available. That would mean that he would have to request less time the following week. I think that's -- if Your Honour recalls, his concern was being away from his position more than one week at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we have -- we have several problems there. First of all, the scheduling for the Judges in various cases. That's one issue. We'll -- we'll consider it, Mr. Groome. But you also are aware that where the medical experts have not said that four hours a week would be impossible for Mr. Stanisic -- four days a week would not be impossible for Mr. Stanisic, at the same time they said introduce that gradually and slowly, and we announced that we would start with three days a week. But we'll consider it. It's too early to really finally form an opinion about it, but it's on the record. Mr. Petrovic, you have noted your five weeks for the agreed facts. You were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that it will be necessary for me to answer, but I thank you for the time permitted, and we will do our best to meet our commitments in that time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one matter which still is to be put on the record, and that is a request by the Stanisic Defence to be granted additional time to respond to the 18th application to amend the 65 ter list. In order to have everything clearly on the record, I'd like to read from the e-mail exchanges. On the 23rd of September, 2010, the Stanisic Defence mailed the following message to Chambers staff: "The Stanisic Defence would like to apply informally for a two-week extension for our response to the Prosecution's 18th application to amend its 65 ter list. The motion is sizable, complex, and requires extensive work to understand its significance and impact on the trial process. Currently, the Stanisic Defence is working at full capacity on issues as far ranging as a 250 bar table motion and the Prosecution's military expert report (500 exhibits) and have no capacity to deal with the aforementioned application to add yet more evidence to the case against the accused. Please would you advise whether this e-mail can stand as our application to extend the usual time limits or whether we need to file something formal." On the 24th of September, Chamber's staff, upon instruction of the Judges, answered by e-mail as follows: "The Judges accept this as a filing and will, on Wednesday, the 29th of September, when the Chamber will hold a housekeeping session, put it on the record. The Chamber would also appreciate if the other parties could respond to this motion preferably before the 29th of September or at the latest on the 29th of September. The Chamber will then consider the motion and issue its decision." Two weeks' extension. Any objections, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not -- may I take it also not from the Simatovic Defence? Then hereby the extension of time is granted as requested, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were my agenda items. What I'd like to do is now to move on to the MFI list, unless there's any other matter. No. Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to remind you once again about Witness Kovacevic and the diary which should have been provided. We don't have information whether the diary was given to the office in Belgrade. Perhaps something slipped by me without knowing. I think the diary should have arrived some two or three weeks ago to the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I think that the latest information - I think it was provided to the parties - was that where it was expected that the diary would be delivered a couple of days late on a Friday that when it was not received on that Friday that then the VWS tried to contact the witness again and that then information was received that he had left home and would be abroad or at least away from home for close to two weeks. And we are constantly monitoring it, and VWS is active in receiving further information. But I've got no further information for you at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If everyone's ready to start with the MFI list. The first one, P18. I'd like to put on the record that in relation to this BBC interview with Vojislav Seselj, that the Stanisic Defence has withdrawn its objections. Mr. Jordash, if we understood you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that the Simatovic has not responded in -- within the time-frame that was set by the Chamber. Under those circumstances, the Chamber admits P18 into evidence. And the Chamber wonders whether, Mr. Groome, there is an update as to the revised translation concerning, if you remember well, that somewhere I think it was "Russian occupation" instead of "Turkish occupation."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The new translation is available. It just needs to be organised between the Registry and Mr. Laugel with respect to -- I believe it's uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It just needs to be replaced. Mr. Laugel informs me that technically he needs -- the Chamber has to order it to be unreleased or released back to the Prosecution so we can upload the corrected translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it could have been uploaded under a different 65 ter number, but let's -- the Chamber admits it into evidence and grants leave to replace the original translation by the newly produced one and allows all technical steps necessary to achieve that. Then we move on. Next one is P51 on my list. The problem there was that the -- as noted on the 1st of September, that paragraph 1 of the English version of the statement given by Mr. Kovacevic did not contain all the information which was found in the B/C/S version. Has a new and full translation been prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it been uploaded, or is it the same problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's going to be the same issue for all of or many of these remaining matters. It's ready. And once the technical aspects are done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you provided a copy to the other parties of the new translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Laugel is checking that now, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps if we could move forward and come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's -- we move forward. I suggest the following. It was just completing a translation. I would like to admit into evidence the exhibit now with new translation and give an opportunity to the Defence to ask the Chamber to revisit the matter within two weeks if there's any problem with this new translation. If that's agreeable, I see Mr. Jordash is nodding yes. Simatovic Defence is still thinking about it. You agree as well? Then P51 is admitted into evidence. The new translation can be uploaded and replace the existing translation, and every technical step needed for that is -- is given leave for being taken. The next one, P378, is not to deal with at this very moment. It relates to the Mladic diary indirectly. I will not deal with the matter at this moment. The next one is P79. But before dealing with P379, I would like to move to P386, which is the analysis of the Main Staff of the VRS, a document which was introduced through Witness Milovanovic, and it's one in a series of documents. The Chamber has invited the parties to reduce the size of what should be admitted from this document, and the Chamber also expressed its awareness that there might be a need then to later again widen the scope of the material contained in this document which is tendered. Mr. Groome, have you, perhaps together with the Defence, defined certain portions of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is my error. We have prepared a reduced -- proposed reduced version of the document but in my error -- it's my oversight that I have not sent that to the Defence. I will send that to them by tomorrow, and I apologise for the delay in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this assists at all, but for us this -- this document, the whole of it is useful, and we can foresee a situation where we're almost certainly going to ask Your Honours to accept all of it in parts. And we would perhaps simply say at this stage that if Your Honours could reconsider whether we can just submit the whole thing now. I remember reading this in preparation for this particular witness and wanting to rely upon a substantial amount of it, even though I didn't put those bits to the witness, or many of those bits to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what's the size of the document? Of course, the Chamber is a bit concerned about being flooded with --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it's about a hundred pages, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Simatovic Defence whether they take a similar position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do take a similar position as Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and in our review, we were only recommending very minimal redactions. We, too, believe that much of the document will be relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you what remains of the hundred pages, 80, or 60, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would have to check. I believe it's -- it would be even less than the -- I believe it will more than the 80 is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More than the 80. Then the whole exercise seems to be rather useless. Let's -- and there were no -- let me see. I know now that the redaction seems to be unsuccessful. I now move back to 379, which is a list of 11 intelligence reports, dated from 1992 to 1995, which is authenticated by the witness Manojlo Milovanovic. Let me see. I think we just dealt with P386 as one of the underlying documents for P379. I do see that the OTP has withdrawn the application with respect to some of the items covered by this list, but the list of intelligence reports remains unaffected. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We still tender 379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections? P379 is admitted into evidence. P386 is also admitted into evidence. We'll not deal with P395 at this moment. P396 is a chart which lists 14 documents, being intelligence reports. The -- one of the issues was whether all the underlying documents were uploaded. I think that in June we established that that was the case. There has been some confusion about whether this was really admitted or not. The transcript seems not to be fully clear. I hereby order that P396 is admitted into evidence and that P396 consists of a chart but includes attached documents to that chart. There was also some -- therefore now also in e-court P396 should show that it is admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, is this sufficient guidance for you? Yes. I see it is. Then P397. There is a -- there was a similar problem, some confusion about whether it was admitted into evidence or not. It's a chart listing 40 documents, again intelligence reports, which were introduced through the witness Milovanovic. Mr. Groome, can you confirm that, as uploaded in e-court, P397 now contains the chart plus the 40 attached documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P397 is admitted into evidence under seal. The next item on the list is P444, which is a list of per diems, per diem payments, which were made to the members of the RDB JATD over various periods of times. That is the matter I think we dealt with under earlier payment records received through RFA 1639. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That is correct. It is -- it includes P444 through P468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- yes. You're right. Now let me just check what we decided earlier when we discussed this matter. I think we asked Madam Registrar to assign numbers to those exhibits which had not yet received exhibit numbers, and further submissions to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's for the purpose of just assigning exhibit numbers marked for identification, I can send an e-mail with a Word table chart to the Registrar for the assignment of numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have not yet reached the stage where we can finally decide on admission. Then I move on to the next item on the MFI list, which is P512, a chart with forensic documentation. The issue there was that what is not found on P512 are the exhibit numbers that are assigned to the documents. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And we have prepared a version of P512 that does contain those exhibit numbers. That has been uploaded as 65 ter 5795.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one of the problems was, I think -- one of the problems was that you can't just -- the original -- the signatures will not be there in original any more. So what I suggest is that the original chart as it was signed by the witness will now be accompanied by the same chart with the additional information that is meanwhile provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's precisely what we've done, Your Honour. We did -- on the chart that we modified, we also redacted Dr. Strinovic's signature so it was clear that we weren't making any changes to anything that had been signed by the witness. But now there's the version signed by Dr. Strinovic and the version with the P numbers on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the additional --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's me see. Now, this also relates to some extent to P722 and following, where I understand there was an issue in relation to -- for at least some of these documents and no English translation be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct. And in fact there are still a few, a very few, that are outstanding. I believe there are three translations that are still outstanding, a couple of translations that we've only received partially for documents that were both English and B/C/S in the original, and then a couple of documents that were just disclosed to the Defence before court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. I think earlier today there was still 40 missing, or something like. But apparently now that number is reduced. Now, although there is a relation between P512 and all these -- all these documents, I think that nothing opposes admission of P512, which is the just the chart with the signatures. If the parties would agree, then it's hereby decided that P512 is admitted into evidence and now contains the two versions of that chart. Therefore, leave is also granted to add that one to P512, as it was earlier marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we leave this matter, could we also ask if the Registry be authorised to unlock the underlying documents as necessary to upload translations as they become available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Leave is granted to -- to link the documents in e-court, and therefore whatever technical measures that requires is hereby granted. Now, I saw this morning that there were still ten translations outstanding. Could you indicate which out of those ten have now been provided? I had on my list this morning 743, 774 are still missing. 801, 802, 816, 840, 859, 862, 867, and 914; that was my list as matters stood this morning as we received it from the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand things at the moment, the three that remain were -- we still have not received the translation are P743, the first one on the list, and then the last two, P867 and P914. We disclosed translations today of P816 and 840. And as to the others, they have been previously disclosed, although in some cases it's only a partial translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I suggest is that you now prepare a full list where 65 ter number and P numbers do appear, because then it's easier to admit them into evidence, and it's also easier for the Defence to formulate any objections. As far as the translations are concerned, how much time would you need after the last translation has been received to review them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have a week, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A week after you have received the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of these, the three outstanding translations. Mr. Farr, if we have not heard within a week, then you can ask, on the basis of that list you have prepared, to -- and it might even be -- that might even be on the basis of P512. I do not know exactly. I don't have any clear recollection what have we find there. But that within a week after that you address the Chamber and that we'll finalise this matter so that finally all the medical documentation is in evidence apart from any objections we have not heard about yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have discussed P943 briefly. Mr. Jordash, you were invited to include that in your observations. That's one of the -- one of the audio -- one of the intercepts. Next one: P967. The Office of the Prosecutor earlier refrained from tendering P967. It was to do something with something that happened in the Martic case. Do you intend to now tender P967?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document that was discussed by Radoslav Maksic during the Martic case but not admitted during his testimony because he was unable to authenticate it. We will tender it from the bar table, I'm happy to make that application now, or we can include it in a future written bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could include it in the bar table motion so that we have always clear charts on -- this is the document, that's the relevance, that's the position of -- of the Defence teams, then if you would include that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to be included in a bar table motion. Next item on my list is P972, report of the commission. We have discussed it in length earlier today, so we don't have to decide on this matter at this very moment. The same is true for P973. Next one is P975 -- no. I can -- I can't deal with that right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll leave P975 for the time being. Next one on the list is P979, where the Chamber expects the Prosecution to provide further information on the document's provenance. And I think, as a matter of fact, that the same is true for P1009, because the two documents stem from the same collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We have sent a Request for Assistance to the government that provided them and we have not received a reply yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not received a reply. When did you send the request?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I'd have to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we would prefer not to leave this pending forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. P1009 is -- the issue was raised on the 20th of September. We will pursue it forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As soon as we have information, we'll provide it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The other one was pending a bit longer. But could you please keep the Chamber updated about the -- well, let's say within four weeks from now to see whether we -- whether you have received any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then the -- the next one is P996, which is an official note of the 30th of March, 1993, signed by Dusan Orlovic. The issue -- well, the conclusion the -- the Prosecution would like the Chamber to draw is that the person who signed this document is the same person, the witness -- and the document was introduced through Witness JF-039, that it's the same person the witness spoke about during his examination. But that does not follow from the answer of that witness. Even if it would be possible to conclude this, it's unclear what purpose the document serves, especially since the witness had answered a question in relation to that already. You have informed us, Mr. Groome, that the document is subject of a pending application for protective measures. The Chamber decided that we deny admission without prejudice. The document does not assist the Chamber in understanding the testimony. That means that if at any other moment for other purposes you want to tender that document, it's -- the decision is without prejudice, but at this moment the admission is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll revisit the issue with respect to the identity and his ability to say it's the same person, but part of the reason the Prosecution tendered it with this witness was that this witness had given evidence about local police being circumvented and reports being made directly to the Serbian DB, and the Prosecution was advancing this by examining the addressee and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber has decided on the matter without prejudice. If there is at any other moment you would like us to -- not to review -- of course, you can always ask to reconsider the decision, but the Chamber was thinking more in terms of other circumstances where it becomes more clear in what way the document would assist the Chamber rather than in relation to the testimony of this witness. I have dealt with P1009. P1010, up to and including P1479 are Theunens documents, and they will have to wait until Mr. Theunens has given his testimony. I am looking at the clock. We have still the D exhibits to deal with. I'm confident that we could do that in one hour, which would mean that there's no 10 or 20 minutes left for other submissions. We'll take a break. And we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now deal with the D exhibits. First one on my list is D3, official note of Emil Cakalic, which is a long-pending story. We last dealt with it on the 22nd of June when the Chamber invited the parties to make a joint filing. Where are we at this moment? Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution and the Defence did meet to discuss this exhibit. There is substantial agreement. There's two matters, and this is similar to the official notes that were discussed earlier today. The Defence is tendering pursuant to Rule 89 the official note that -- of Mr. Cakalic. Then the Prosecution is seeking to have certain transcript portions from the Milosevic case also admitted. Where we last left it was for the Simatovic Defence to check just the small portion of the Milosevic transcript that the Prosecution also wanted included and then get back to us. The Prosecution, at this time, if the Simatovic Defence prepares a joint filing, we will look at it and hopefully resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, your principal objection against admitting into evidence official notes, a way of circumventing the Rules, is -- does that apply here as well, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first I wanted to say something concerning what my learned friend said. We responded on 1 July precisely on what parts of the Milosevic transcript we were concerned with. We identified the pages important to us from the Milosevic case. I thought that matter was cleared. We sent an e-mail to Mr. Groome on the 1st of July on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There has been e-mail exchanges, and I believe that there was just one portion of the Milosevic testimony that was not included that the Prosecution also wanted included from that e-mail. We're happy to discuss this and look at the e-mails, and I believe that this can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You're close to a solution. You've got three weeks to further discuss the matter and file a joint filing or file it in good co-ordination and agreement with each other. If you have not resolved this matter in three weeks, the first day after that -- let me see. That is -- I look at my agenda. I haven't got my agenda. At the earliest possibility after these three weeks, if you have not resolved the matter, you're invited to meet me at 7.00 in the morning in my Chambers where I can assist you in seeing whether we can overcome any practical problems. We'll wait and see what the Chamber receives in the next three weeks. Of course, parties are still free to take their own positions, but just to overcome any practical problems for this matter which is now pending for almost a year without a clear explanation for that. The next one is D25, the -- and D25 is under seal, as is D26. Further submissions are expected by the Chamber. I think it was after you would have had access to the relevant files. I'm not going into too much details because the documents are under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, a member of the Prosecution team has examined the file, and the Prosecution has no basis for believing that the criminal file is anything other than what it purports to be. The Prosecution withdraws its objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that it's ready. I take it, Mr. Jordash, that you have no -- no, no. I don't know even who filed it, who -- but both Defence teams are in agreement. D25 and D26 are admitted under seal. Next one on my list is D55, which is related to D56 and to be considered together with D70 from -- these are all documents -- Yes, Mr. Jordash. Perhaps I give you the floor to further explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For reasons that I don't need to go into, it's completely my fault that this hasn't been done. I can commit to doing this and have it to Your Honours by Friday. I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By this Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: By this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is true for both D55, D fifty --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- six and D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- six and D70.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is on the record. Then we have a list. A series of documents, D60 to D66. Oral submissions have been made by the Prosecution in relation to these documents. The Simatovic Defence at the time, which was on the 22nd of June, indicated that it was not ready to respond. And then we invited the Prosecution to put brief submissions with regard to the relevance of these documents, to put them in writing. And then the Defence to respond in writing. Where do we stand in relation to these documents which are mainly background documents for the witness Sliskovic? Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As Your Honour has noted, we've stated our position on the record orally. We can file this same submission in writing. It is on the record and very clear. With respect to the exhibits, the Simatovic Defence is the proponent of it, so I'm not sure if they want to look at what our oral submission was and then file it and we can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I recollect correctly, and -- we checked that on the agenda of the last session of this type. Perhaps I wasn't all too familiar with the agenda then and may not have seen it come in, but I believe you asked the OTP to submit a written submit. I asked my learned friend Mr. Groome during one of our meetings when I was to receive that submission. Mr. Groome promised it would follow soon. Two weeks ago, we tried to remind the OTP by having sent an e-mail, asking that we receive their position on these two documents so that we would be in a position to reply. We still have not received it. If you are going to vary your order, we can go back to the part of the transcript to see what Mr. Groome actually stated in his argument and then to respond, but I believe your order was specific to the OTP to submit a written submission and then we were in turn to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was our instruction, but I'll just check that on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I accept that that was your instruction, Your Honour. I apologise. And we -- if the Chamber will give us leave until tomorrow afternoon, I will have a written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Tomorrow afternoon. How much time would you then need to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope not more than a week. Seven days. I will also strive to do it even more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I set the deadline for it: 11th of October, which is Monday, so that if you do not finally manage to do it next week, then at least you have the weekend left to finish it. We then move on to D69. That was a matter of translation. I do understand that the Simatovic Defence has uploaded the translation into e-court in -- on the 19th of July. Mr. Groome, any problems as far as the uploaded translation is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection to the translation, Your Honour. And I neglected to check whether we -- whether we had any other objection. I -- I accept that the Chamber will -- may rule on it, and if I feel the need to re -- ask the Chamber to reconsider its decision, I will do that at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Registrar, the uploaded translation, which is, if I'm not mistaken, is 2D01-0536, can be attached to D69, and D69 is admitted into evidence. We have dealt with D70, where we will receive further information. D75, translation issue. Only an informal translation was available when the document was introduced. The English translation is now received, as we were informed on the 12th of July. Any problems with this translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the English translation which was received, do you have it or -- because I don't see immediately here a 65 ter number. Have you received the English translation which should be linked to D75? Could --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is uploaded at 1D269.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the translation, or is that the document itself? Because I have here 1D00269, but I -- I thought it was linked to D -- to D75 and not to the English translation of that, but if you could clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the translation. Madam Registrar, could you confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is the translation, Your Honours. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. You may link the English translation to D75. And D75 is admitted into evidence. The next item is D79, a letter from the SDA headquarters titled "Information On Full Readiness of Connection and Following of SDA," date, 20th of September, 1991. The OTP had this document on its list. The Simatovic Defence used the document with Witness JF-002. The OTP questions the authenticity of the document. The Chamber would like to hear from the parties as soon as possible as to whether the questions about the authenticity stand, whether they stand or do not stand. That was, I think, what was asked already, but we have not received any response to that. At least not as far as I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I recollect well, it was upon the Prosecution to check where the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the document was on the OTP 65 ter list, but I think the document was produced in another case by a Defence team. We asked for more information about it, also about the view of the Prosecution, whether they would still challenge the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We cannot provide any additional information because, as noted, it was provided by a Defence team on a different case. So we have no way to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you receive it from that Defence team and did then the Simatovic Defence take it from your 65 ter list, or did you get it from the other Defence team? And what was the fate of this document in the other case? Was there any challenge to the authenticity? What -- we'd like to get more body on the subject so that we are better able to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was admitted in the other case. I could look for that. So -- so could the Defence, and they are the ones putting forth the document, but I can undertake that for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had it on your 65 ter list, which means that you considered it to be used as an exhibit, which at least suggests that you would know something about the document. And now to challenge the authenticity of a document which you once intended to use comes as a little surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can repeat -- what I stated on that day was that we were asked to provide the origin regularly for our exhibits because that is the way to ensure the highest level of reliability. So even when we tender something from our exhibit list, we do provide information on origin. Aside from that, the document is, I would argue, not directly relevant to the witness anyway. It's not highly problematic for us. But the origin is also uncertain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be -- let's be very practical. Either you further explore the matter, and of course it's the Defence who tenders this document and is expected, therefore, to respond to any challenge to the authenticity. You could ask where the other Defence team got it from or whatever. Now, we can do two things: Either to explore the matter in further detail and then I can set a deadline, because otherwise we'll be in the same position in December and then in January, which is not what the Chamber prefers to do. So either the Chamber receives further submissions. Or in the alternative, if the Defence says, "Well, we're not fully convinced on the authenticity yet, but we're not making -- we're not breaking our legs over it," then, of course, then the objection would be gone. So either of the two. Either we fully explore it, or we leave it behind us. And that is not only true for the Prosecution but also the Defence. If that is not only to -- for the Prosecution, but also for the Defence. If you find the document important enough to -- to persist in its being admitted, then you also have to further explore the background of this document, which is of unknown source. Is that clear? The deadline is two weeks from now. Yes? If any of the -- yes. If we don't receive any further information from either party, this might lead to a decision that the document is not admitted. I just don't want these matters which are not the most important ones not to be kept on the MFI list forever. That's -- either it's important to pay attention to it or it's not important enough. And then the party who still insists and has paid attention to it will have the favour -- have the advantage of -- of having it in, or, in the other case, not to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I'm afraid the onus of doing the research now lies with us. Unless someone speaks out, if I understood correctly, it would not be admitted, hence the Prosecutor, disputing the document in any case, have nothing to do. On my behalf, I will contact the Defence team in the Samac case and I will try to identify the counsel procuring it. I will do my utmost, although I believe it is far easier for the OTP to access the exhibit list on -- of that case. I apologise again for perhaps speaking freely, but I'm afraid all I can do is to try and research the source and what counsel procured it. And then the Prosecution can check whether in the other case that document was admitted or not. That is my proposal. And then that could be done within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps also whether the authenticity was contested in the other case. That is, of course, important information. That -- I'm not trying to put the ball on -- on your part of the -- of the playground, Mr. Bakrac. I think the Prosecution has not been serious enough in further exploring the basis for its challenge to the authenticity. That's one. And the Defence has not seriously further elaborated and researched what the source of the document is and, therefore, positively contributing to a finding that it is an authentic document. So both on the tendering side and on the challenging side more serious attempt is needed. Otherwise, we are here again in a couple of months from now, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. You're completely right. I can only reiterate, without contradicting your words and without seeking an excuse, but the only source we have is the OTP's 65 ter list. If the Prosecutor puts a list -- a document on their list and later on asserts that the document is not authentic, then that is less than serious. If we need to check each and every 65 ter document if the Prosecution no longer likes the provenance of that document, then the burden is entirely upon us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's certainly not my position, that you have to -- to verify the authenticity of all the documents you intend to use and which appear on the -- on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. But once an issue has been raised about authenticity and if it comes from a Defence team in another case, then I think both parties should make a serious effort. And then we'll see how this will end. I return to D75. Yes. Could I just verify. We were talking about the newly uploaded -- no. Let me see. It was not a -- yes. Two English translations have been uploaded under number 1D269. One is attached at this moment to D75; it may well be that that was the informal translation which was the only one at the time and that the one which is not attached now, is not linked, is the new one. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, therefore, 1D269, which is linked, should be separated from D75. And the other one, 1D269, which is not linked at this moment, should then be attached to D75. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move on to D81. There was no translation available at the time the D81 was MFI'd, pending translation. We do understand that the English translation has now been uploaded. Could you confirm that the translation is uploaded under number 2D01-0643, Madam Registrar. It's confirmed. The English translation under the number I just mentioned can be linked to D81. D81 is admitted into evidence. I move to D85 [Realtime transcript read in error "D81"], which is the statement of Garaplija, dated the 6th of September, 1998, which was tendered through Witness JF-002. The Stanisic Defence wished to tender paragraph 15 of this document. The witness said that the document is false and complete nonsense. Ms. Friedman, you dealt with the matter at the time. You -- we did not have much time at that time to hear further objections. Would you further -- would you wish to further elaborate, or is it -- is -- are your words that -- that this is an out-of-court statement and that the witness is -- that the person who gave this statement is not there to affirm it and that the witness who testifies about it says it's completely false and there's no indicia of reliability? That is what you said. Do you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I would only add what was mentioned again earlier today, that such statements may be reliable if there's a witness who can attest to the indicia of reliability, as with the commission witnesses, for example; but, yes, in this case there are no indicia of reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
